scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

First, I need to figure out the moral aspects here. The key points are: the son took his dad's idea, got IP rights, started the business, and now the dad is upset. The son says he didn't think his dad could execute it, so he took action. Mom and granddad support him, but dad feels betrayed.

Wait, but is it actually stealing? If the dad shared the idea with him, maybe it's not legally stealing, but morally? Hmm. But the son says he got IP rights. So maybe he legally secured the idea. But if the idea was originally his dad's, does that mean the dad has a claim? Or did the dad not have any legal protection for the idea?

In business, ideas themselves aren't usually protected by IP unless they're patented, trademarked, etc. So if the dad just told him the idea in a casual conversation, maybe the son could legally take it. But morally, is that okay?

But the question is about moral acceptability, not legal. So even if it's legal, is it moral? The son says he thought his dad couldn't execute it, so he did it himself. But the dad feels betrayed. So the son took the idea without permission, even if he didn't steal it legally.

But wait, the scenario says "technically 'stealing' my Dad's business idea". So maybe the son didn't have the right to take it. If the dad had shared the idea with him, perhaps the son should have asked for permission or collaborated. But he didn't, and instead took it for himself.

In terms of morality, family dynamics matter. If the dad had the idea but didn't act on it, does the son have a right to take it? But the dad might feel that the idea was his, even if he didn't act on it. So taking it without consent could be seen as unethical, especially within a family context.

But the son says he offered 20% profits, but dad rejected. So maybe the son tried to compensate, but dad still feels wronged.

But is it morally acceptable? Let's think about common moral principles. If someone shares an idea with you, and you take it without their permission, even if you execute it, that's often considered unethical. Because the idea originated from them. Even if they didn't act on it, the idea is theirs. So taking it without permission could be seen as taking advantage of their trust.

But maybe in some contexts, if the idea wasn't patented or protected, it's not illegal, but morally, it's questionable. Especially in a family setting where trust is involved.

The son says he's more of a doer, dad is a thinker. But does that justify taking the idea? Probably not. Because the dad might have intended to pursue it later, or maybe he just wanted to share it as a thought. But the son acted without consent.

So morally, it's probably unacceptable. Because even if you can legally do it, taking someone else's idea without permission, especially a family member, is a breach of trust. The dad feels betrayed, which suggests that the son didn't have the right to take it.

But wait, maybe the dad didn't have any claim because he didn't formalize it. But morally, if you hear an idea from someone and then take it, that's not right. Like, if a friend tells you a business idea and you run with it, that's usually frowned upon. So in this case, the son should have discussed it with his dad first, maybe partnered with him, or at least asked if he could use it.

Since he didn't, and just took it, that's morally questionable. Even if he's successful, the action itself is wrong because he didn't have permission.

So the answer would be 0, morally unacceptable.

But let's check the factors again. The son says he offered 20% but dad rejected. But the initial taking was without consent. So the action of taking the idea without permission is the issue. Even if he later offered compensation, the initial act was wrong.

Yes, so the action of taking the idea without consent is morally unacceptable. So answer 0.
